utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have that of the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel from Zagreb, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, Michael Greaves, Defence attorney from Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think the witness is still under cross-examination. Can we have the next Defence counsel cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours, it is my turn to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still under oath. WITNESS J (continued) Cross-examined by MR. OLUJIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. J.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the witness does not have the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You are now in The Hague for the second day. You have been in The Hague here for the second day now, I hope that you will return home soon. I represent Mr. Zdravko Mucic. We will have a conversation here, and I would like to request, even though we speak similar languages, they are different languages but we understand one another -- for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, for all of us present in the courtroom, I would like to request that you wait until I have finished asking you a question and when you hear the end of the interpretation to one of the official languages, then please proceed with your answer. Did we understand each other on this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday during your examination-in-chief, you said that you were from the Celebici camp for four months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the camp, you who were imprisoned there, did you have the morning parades or the morning roll calls with also salute to the flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no roll calls, no reading of the names and no salute to the flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there guard parades in the camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you were there for four months, did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see any of that, not for the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a satisfactory answer to me. Mr. J, can you tell me, how many times did you see Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him on a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, "a number of times"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of times, it was not once or twice, three times, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic have a certain rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that is not my question. My question is whether he had a certain rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did wear a uniform, I did not notice a rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, you say that Mr. Mucic wore a uniform. What types of uniforms did you see in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there different uniforms there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point, I saw Mr. Delic wearing a black uniform. I once saw the soldiers when they were there in training, they had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards in the camp also carry weapons outside of their guard posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean inside the camp or in the compound?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts among the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes there were quarrels, yes, they were quarreling sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, you served the JNA army, right, in the JNA army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give an oath there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how to disassemble a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very well. In fact, I was taken out several times to clean a rifle, but I needed help of Sejo to help me do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this Sejo somebody who was there with you in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am asking you about your military service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was serving in the JNA, I had the M48 rifle, that was the old one, and then I was a cook, so we only did it for the first three months and then afterwards I was just cooking. I was in Montenegro. We were eight cooks who were working in shifts. When you did not work then you slept and then you worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the rifle that you used to have, you knew how to shoot it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the training, yes, then I would shoot from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell, you said that you were in the training, you gave the oath to the JNA. How were you trained? Can you sign a capitulation document, capitulation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that, but the oath was that I pledge to defend the country and for the rest, people did not ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say you do not know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not, I mean the oath was to defend Yugoslavia. If there should be an attack, if Yugoslavia was attacked, then I pledged to defend the country and to if necessary give my, even, life to it. That is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taught that if you were taken prisoner that you would do everything to try to set yourself free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that you did not learn that during your training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and nobody ever mentioned that, I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in the training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just three months, the first three months. It was both training plus training for the cook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have like political training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, you were born in Bradina, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Bradina, was there general People's Defence system there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the municipality level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the municipality. There was something at the municipality level, I do not know, the People's Defence, or the Civilian Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a commander in Bradina, a commander who was in charge of the defence and everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, we practically did not have an army, we had -- it was just talked about if there would be an attack, then we will not touch anyone, if somebody attacked Muslims, if some army came, we would protect them and some people went to some, I do not know, negotiations or some agreements making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So does that mean that you did have a commander in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a small group which was going to some kind of negotiations or talks there, I was not part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was, then? Just for example, one or two names, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that on one occasion there was somebody -- maybe Rusmo, who came from Konjic for those negotiations. I know there was a meeting in the community halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Rusmo from Konjic, who from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Rajko or Raso Djordjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Djordjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, did you have any weapons in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some weapons in Bradina, some rifles. A few people had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A small rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something significant, a few people carried them. I know that there was something there, a few people had a few things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many weapons do you think it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trust me, I do not know. I was taking care of my business and I did not want to take part in all that, because I did not even expect anything to happen. I did not want to be involved. Maybe in that sense I was a bit isolated, I was on the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my own personal weapons which I got from the former authorities. I had a rifle and I had a pistol and this pistol was stolen about three or four months -- as I bought it, I had never used it, it was in the new house and it was hidden in the sofa and I think that I even know who stole it from me. I went and I reported it was stolen and I say -- I told them that I think I knew who did it and they said, "what shall we do?", I said, "bring him round, confront him", but they said if they bring him and he said he did not do it, and that is the end of that, "why do we not just take it easy and proceed and we will get to who actually stole it".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had a rifle and a pistol. What was the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Karabin, I do not know exactly, that was also with a permit. That has been a long time in my possession and as far as a pistol is concerned, there was Tucakovic, who was the deputy commander in Konjic who was sitting in my cafe and he said "why do you not apply to get a rifle?", and I said "why", because he said "almost everybody who has not been criminally prosecuted can do it, so you can get it". So I got it and when I reported that it had disappeared, I think I also had 25 bullets on that permit, so I never touched it, I never even tested it. I know it was a Zastava, make 62.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so you had a rifle and a pistol. When did you ask for these weapons? When was the permit issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a rifle for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is actually a rifle that belonged to my father, so when my father died, I took it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you applied for the pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three or four months before the war, the pistol disappeared, the window was broken and the weapon was gone. I did not go to the court, I just went to the police station and made a report and I told them, "I think it is this young man took it". I said, "why do you not bring him over, so I can confront him?" They said, "if we bring him here now and then ask him and he denies, then that is the end of the story so we cannot pursue it any longer. The way we normally do it is we do it slowly"; but it was never resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how much ammunition did you get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 75 bullets. That was with the bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much ammunition did you have for the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any. That was more like a trophy type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, when you were in Celebici, you described all the torture that you were subjected to. Did you ever go to Mr. Mucic officially and officially complain about what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I did not dare complain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me about these weapons that you had, the rifle and the pistol. Where were these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the old house. Both the pistol and the rifle were hidden in a sofa in the new house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were hidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hidden from the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if I came in I would not know where it was, that is how I understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was hiding them from the children so that, God forbid, the children would find it. The rifle did not have bullets but the pistol did, so then when the pistol was stolen from me, it was together, both together, in the same place, both the pistol and the rifle. However, the person who stole the pistol left the rifle there, so then I took the rifle and then I moved it to the old house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this rifle taken away later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a permit for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a permit for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were in the camp, you said you were limited as to the movements around the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now Mr. J, when the Red Cross arrived, were you still limited in your movements or could you move around freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were still limited in our movements, but it was a bit easier, it was a different thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during your examination-in-chief that Mr. Mucic was present when you were put in the container, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was present there because I was looking ahead of me and I was -- it was a big stress and it was beating and I think I may have seen him there. I am not going to claim 100 per cent that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are allowing for a possibility that he was not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw him there, but -- I thought he was there, because they started beating me there, but I thought I heard his voice there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you this question, Mr. J, because all other prisoners who were there said that Mr. Mucic was not present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may interrupt to correct the record, I believe there is a significant amount of testimony that Mr. Mucic was there when people were put in the manhole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that voice very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: All right, but you are not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certain about the voice, that is 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief when my learned colleague asked you questions, you mentioned that there were some Arab journalists in the camp, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some Arabs there, they were journalists, they were dark complexion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What country did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Arabs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because everybody was saying Arabs, Arabs were coming, Arabs were here, both the guards and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you speak Arabic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the guards said that the Arabs -- that these were Arabs and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, you saw them, but how did you conclude that they were Arabs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had dark complexions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you recognised them racially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also they spoke this strange language, and the guards right after that said, "these are Arabs".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, were you a member of the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of the Communist League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you mentioned Mr. Guska. Were you friends with Mr. Guska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the last day. He was a vet, and he inspected meat in my own slaughterhouse, so there were three or four vets who were taking turns every day or maybe a week, every week, so that we probably sat together at least 100 times, either in my cafe or in my butcher's shop. I also knew his mother. He would come to me and I thought we were friends. I think up until then, he showed nothing, for instance that he would never do anything hostile to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when did that friendship break up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Bradina, he was in Konjic and just before the war, I think, I do not know how long before the war, he was appointed a commander of the police. Up until then he worked as a vet and then on the eve of the war he was appointed to the chief of police in Konjic. We never came to quarrel, but when things fell apart and when I was brought to Bradina, I saw him there and there were a lot of people there, a lot of -- Sevko was there and a lot of soldiers and I sensed, I think that he, even sort of hid a little bit from me. I think that he was a bit, you know -- he apparently did not want to just come and face me, but Sevko was there, Guska was there and Sevko said, "why did you run away? You had so much money, why did you run away?", you know. Then he said, "tie up this garbage" and I know the person very well, he was a policeman before the war, he went down to an old house belonging to some Pero and then he brought some wire from it with pliers and then they tied us, tied our hands, because then they took us to the intersection and there was my house and Sevko and Guska was right in front of my house and then there was Mehmed Alija there, but in any event they took us to some storage room to kill us, there was a little fountain, and they wanted to take us there. I saw Ira, a lot of people, some Gajic, there was Osman Gajic, Hodza Rizvic, his son Miso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Miso, Hodza's son, when we came to this very entrance, we were ordered to stop, I saw Diksa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. J. It is not necessary to go that wide. If you could please just stick to the question that I ask of you and if you can please answer as succinctly as possible, so that you would not also tire too much. I understand that it is difficult for you, but you also please try to understand us. We are also doing our job here in the courtroom. Yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, you said that, virtually up to the last moment, you went to Konjic before war broke out, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Konjic, and Tarcin. I went to purchase goods and cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much before the shelling of Konjic? How many days before that did you go to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea, I cannot remember exactly when Konjic was attacked. I do not know. I went regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, you have no idea? You did not know that Konjic was attacked and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know it was attacked before Bradina was attacked, before we were attacked in Bradina. I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Bradina was attacked, did you defend yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People started to flee when Bradina was attacked. The shells starting falling very suddenly and the women and children --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the attack on Bradina last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I know it started somewhere in the afternoon, it lasted all evening, all night, and the next day I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore more than two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not two days. People started fleeing immediately, within an hour, I think, something like that. I know that in my old house, I was in my old house with my wife and children at the time, and I know that children from that side where people were being killed, the women and children were fleeing and they came to my cellar and there were more than 30 women and children in the cellar that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. J, yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned that when you were leaving Celebici, Mr. Zara and Mr. Pavo were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who else went with you to Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody called -- there was a small car, a small Fiat and a van and both were full of people. There were three cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was the trip from Celebici to where you were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite long, we went through Butrovic Polje, then I think it was Kresevo, I know we went through Kiseljak, through the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain more closely, was it about 100 kilometres? Roughly, 90, 100, 110?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know what the distance was, but I know it was not close, because we went from Donje Selo, Butrovic Polje, then via Kravulja, then there was a road through the woods and then we got to Kiseljak somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went through the woods. What were the conditions on the road like, was there snow, torrents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we crossed the stream, I remember, and there was a bridge across the stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there snow, was there a blanket of snow already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic cross with you into Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he separate from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three vehicles got to in front of a house just under Kobiljaca. It was to the left of the road, and we got there, in front of that house, and we all got out and that is when Mucic returned. He came with us to that house and then he turned back. A man in that house had an old Skoda car and he transported some people. Some went on foot, because the man did not have much fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did this trip last, all in all, because obviously it was a long journey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not stop anywhere, we stopped only once in a wood, I think that Pavo went out, I think it was merely to urinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not come across any checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some checkpoints at Butrovic Polje, or when we left Butrovic Polje, yes, we did, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who manned those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army, Mr. J?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Troops in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not ask us anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were wearing uniforms, Zara and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo gave us the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you allow for the possibility that that was the reason why they did not stop you at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they did not stop the other two vehicles either. Nobody even saw us. It was very early in the morning, nobody paid any attention whether we were in uniform or not. Nobody really looked closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. J, I have finished my cross-examination. Thank you, your Honours, that brings to an end my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MORAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic in this case and I am going to ask you a few questions and some of the questions are going to call for a yes or no answer. Can we make an agreement with each other that you will listen to the questions and, if you do not understand them, tell me you do not understand them and I will rephrase it or do whatever is necessary so you do understand. Will you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In return, would you answer just the question that I ask and not something else? If you do that, it will go a whole lot easier for us, sir. Can we agree that you will do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. One other thing, a couple of times yesterday you nodded when you wanted to say yes or no. If you look directly in front of you, you will see a lady in a beige suit and a funny little machine; she is what is called a court reporter. She is taking down everything you say, there is another lady off to your right, and they cannot take a nod. They write down everything we say here. If you answer verbally, yes or no, that will be great. Could you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born, where, in Bradina, in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo, in the district called Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then moved to Bradina, when, when you were a relatively young man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a child, my father was working, he had his business in Bradina, at Ivan Sedlo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have lived basically your entire life in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spent my whole life in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back in, what was it, March or April 1992, there was a referendum in Bosnia over independence. Do you recall the fact that the referendum occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do recall the fact that it occurred, that is what I am asking at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: God knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I am going to ask you now is this, sir. I am going to ask you whether you could have voted, that is what I am asking. I am not asking whether you did vote and I am not asking how you voted, because that is your business and not mine. I am just asking you, could you have voted in that referendum if you so chose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone could have voted, I think there was some sort of a vote, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everybody in Bradina could have voted in that referendum if they had chosen to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Thank you very much, sir. Sir, yesterday on your direct examination, you talked to Ms. McHenry the Prosecutor about an incident where you were being beaten by a group of people and someone at the back of the group said, "that is enough". Do you recall that incident and that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You thought that it was Mr. Delic that was at the back and said, "that is enough", but it was not, it was a guy named Ismet, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Ismet, known as Broceta, who was a commander at the sports hall in Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that beating occurred at Celebici, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the beating was in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when someone said "that is enough", you thought it was Mr. Delic and it turned out later Ismet told you it was him, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that led you to mistake Ismet for Mr. Delic, was it the voice or their physical appearance or some combination of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nighttime, and as Delic was always there within the compound, I somehow thought that he must have been with them, because somebody said, "that is enough" and I thought it was him, because I doubt if one of the guards had said that that it would have had any effect. I did not see Ismet, I could not see Delic either, but I heard somebody saying, "that is enough" and when I was -- and in my subconscious, Delic noticed that somebody had beaten me because I was limping and on one occasion he asked me, "has somebody been beating you?", and I said no, thinking that he was there, but it was not him when I was transferred to Musala, I had always kept it in my mind that it was him, but when I was transferred to Musala, Ismet came and said, "you see, they would have killed you if it had not been for me. Did you hear me say 'that is enough'?" Then I realised it was him, it must have been him, because he used the exact same words, because it was Ismet and not Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying Mr. Ismet does not necessarily look like Mr. Delic and he does not sound like Mr. Delic, you just kind of assumed that it was Mr. Delic because someone was there, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we were terrified. What I am trying to say is that I was beaten so badly, I was so frightened and I heard somebody say, "that is enough" and I thought it was Delic and I believed it had been him until I got to Musala; see, I am telling the truth, that is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody is saying you are not telling the truth, sir. Basically you just heard a voice of authority and you thought it was Hazim, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. That was just what I was trying to get at, sir. Let us go on to something else. In tunnel 9, when you were talking about the conditions, I do not recall whether you said it yesterday, but remember when you gave that statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre in Belgrade, you talked about the conditions in the tunnel were so bad that you and the rest of the people that were in the tunnel were literally sitting in your own excrement; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some such cases, the people who were near the bottom, sitting near the part that was used as a toilet, so at the bottom of the tunnel, people -- it is true that people were sitting in their excrement, because it was not cleaned, and as people relieved themselves, there was more and more of it and it climbed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified, or told the people in Belgrade at least, that things like it was so filthy that if a spoon fell on that floor with all the excrement on it, you had to pick up that spoon and eat with it; do you remember telling them that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do and that was how it was, because it was so filthy everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, while you were in that tunnel, how many cases of cholera were there, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking of the disease?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am thinking of the disease cholera. Did you see anybody with cholera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not and it is a wonder there were not any such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody with typhus, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anyone. We spoke amongst ourselves that if anyone got hepatitis, we would all die. That was the conversation we had amongst ourselves, but it must have been a miracle it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my next question. There were not any cases of hepatitis, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were not, but we were terrified that somebody would get it under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. In fact, it is probably, what would you agree with me, that it is a one in a billion chance that you all did not get hepatitis or cholera or typhus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that question unless there is some showing that this witness is some sort of medical expert who would know such information. I think it is just unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me go ahead on that, your Honour. You, sir, are a butcher by trade, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a butcher, do you actually slaughter your own animals, or did you, back then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My own, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of your training as a butcher is cleanliness around this meat, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, if you do not keep the meat clean and you let the various bodily fluids of the animal get all over it, people will get sick from that, will they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. If when you slaughter an animal, you let bodily fluids and various things from the animal get all over the meat, when someone eats that meat, they can get sick from it, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A vet has to inspect the meat first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, to make sure it is clean and the animal was healthy and things like that, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that the meat is healthy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So part of your training as a butcher and dealing with food products was in cleanliness and the kinds of diseases that you can get by being around unclean, unsanitary things, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it is the vet who examines the meat, because we cannot tell exactly where the meat came from. You buy it at the market, so when we left the camp, there were few people that did not undergo treatment after being discharged. Lots of people reacted positively to the TBC test and had to be treated. I did too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, that is not what counsel is asking. He said in premises where the meat is sold, you appreciate it has to be kept clean all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you are experienced in diseases that can be caused by that, by filth and bad conditions, things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as cattle is concerned, yes. I know a little about man too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as people are concerned, because if they are around this kind of stuff and they eat it, they get sick, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people get sick, some people survive, things that one could never dream of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to where we started this. You testified that it was a miracle that there was a not a lot of disease in that tunnel, among the people in the tunnel, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not examine them. How do we know whether they fell sick or not? We did not move around much either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us go on to something else, sir. The Arab journalists that visited the camp. You talked about them to people in Sarajevo and you talked about those folks to the Office of the Prosecutor, and frankly, some of the things you said in your statements were a little unclear to me. Let me see if we can clear them up. Did those Arab journalists film you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I personally was being beaten, they were not filming, but I think they filmed me washing a heifer. Whether it was a journalist or reporter, I do not know, but the Arabs were there in front of the entrance to the camp, right to the left of the gate on the steps and then they took out those two people and they interrogated them or something like that, and then they would hit them a little too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, the Arab journalists would hit these people, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The people who were bringing them out in front of the Arab journalists, they were hitting, Milosevic and Rajko Djordjic were brought out, as far as I saw, and I saw the reporters to the left when you go into number 9, to the left, next to the steps. Some of them were peeping inside, others were standing. The door was open, and I heard them raising the level of their voices, as if they were ready to hit us. In any case, they raised the level of their voices, they were speaking out loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who is "they"? Is "they" the guards and the camp staff, or is "they" the Arab journalists, or is it some combination of the two of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Arab journalists were right in front of number 9 to the left, they had cameras, some of them were standing, some of them were crouching. I remember they took out Rajko Djordjic, they questioned him in front of the door, "when would the war end?", and this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I said "they", is "they" the Arab journalists who took out Rajko Djordjic, or was it the guards who took out Rajko Djordjic so he could be questioned in front of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic and the other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. That was what I was trying to get at. So if they were beaten -- when they were beaten, these Arab journalists could have seen it, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were filming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw them filming this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I saw them. What they did with it, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let us go on to something else. Let us talk about the International Committee for the Red Cross and when they visited you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, let us move on to that. Do you remember telling Regis Abribat, an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor, that the Red Cross official was a Frenchman and he had a Croatian interpreter; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you told the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor that after you told the Red Cross person and his interpreter, this woman, that you had been beaten, she told the camp guards; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody must have told them, because they repeated the same words we had used. It was either Zara or she, one of the two of them, I cannot say 100 per cent it was her because I did not see her telling them, but somebody must have told them, because when they left, Zara was taken out and all this was within 10 or 15 minutes, they were in number 6 and we were being beaten in front of number 9. We were taken out to strip to the waist, "you are going sunbathing" and then we had to sit next to the wall in front of number 9. It was a very high wall, we had to sit down with our hands behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have discussed that. Let us talk about something along those lines. So when you told the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor that the beating was "because the Red Cross interpreter, who was a Croat, had told the camp authorities that, which had informed the Red Cross representatives, that we were being mistreated", you were just guessing, right? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assuming, because if I did not exactly see her doing it, I cannot claim it, but it is interesting some of the things we said, who had been killed, how they were starving us, how we did not have any water and so on, so they were mentioning those same words when they were beating us and how could they have known when the guards were not there when we were being questioned, because they said the guards would not be allowed to be present, nor anyone on the part of the camp authorities. They told us to speak freely, and when we did, when they left, they said they would be coming back in two days time and we were terribly beaten after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you told the OTP what I just read to you, that it was the Croat interpreter for the French Red Cross representative that told the camp authorities, you were just guessing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assuming that somebody must have told them because only a very short time had gone by, because when they left number 9, this French man and the interpreter, then Zara followed them and when Zara came back, they took us out, so somebody must have told them. How could they know that they were starving us, how much food we got every day, so everything was quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Sir, remember when we started off, you said you were going to listen to my questions and answer my questions. Sir, sometimes, to coin a phrase, I will ask you what time it is and you tell me how a watch works. If you just listen to the question and answer it, this will go a whole lot quicker for all of us, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, as I recall, you also told the Office of the Prosecutor that the Red Cross representatives must have heard you being beaten. Do you remember telling the OTP that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that he could have seen it, because he was in number 6, but the next time when they came two days later, he said that he would come in two or three days, and that did indeed happen, so when he came and when we saw them at the door, we all just fell silent and nobody wanted to talk to them at all, because we were afraid that we would be treated the same way. So we just waited for them to leave. It is not their fault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, so when you told the Office of the Prosecutor that you were sure that the Red Cross representatives heard your cries because afterwards one of them came to see what had happened, that did not occur, or they did not hear your cries? What is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said, I do not remember saying that, that they heard our moans or something, but they were in number 6 and we were in number 9 and there were two guards between number 6 and number 9, that I know because that I saw when we were brought out, they were out there on some grass. I am not saying -- I did not say that he came that day, that may have been misunderstood. He came two days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is fine. Also, on your direct examination, you testified that some time relevant to this trial, right before you were arrested, during the time you were in custody, you had seen Zejnil Delalic's older brother Dzafo around; do you remember testifying to that during direct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not during the examination-in-chief, I do not know if it was Dzafo, that I do not know for sure, but I can describe him, I saw him down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is down, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see Zejnil Delalic, I did not say that during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us go right back to Bradina and the people there. As I understood your testimony, there was no real military organisation there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, can I just, to clear up the transcript, I do not know if there is an interpretation error or if in fact the witness says it, but what the transcript says the witness says: "I did not see Zejnil Delalic. I did not say that during examination-in-chief." I just wonder if counsel could clear up, is it Dzafo he is talking about or Zejnil? I think the transcript is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us clear it up. You knew the Delalic brothers from before the war, all of them, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not well, I knew Sefik the best, because Sefik came to my cafe with Guska and with others. He was the younger one, he must have been there at least 100 times. What I said is that I said that I did not see Zejnil during the main examination, I saw him later. Mira was there, but I saw the brother, I was sitting outside on the grass, and I saw him passing towards the storage -- the warehouse, and he was in a uniform and trousers and some boots and he was coming from the gates. Once I saw him coming from the gate and once towards the gate. This was parallel to number 9, that is the road that was passing number 9, so if this is number 9 (indicates) that road there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On cross-examination with Ms. Residovic yesterday, you said that person was, as I recall, you said that person was Dzafo, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, I know the youngest brother, I know his name for sure, that is what I said yesterday. I know that he had another brother, whether this was Dzafo or not, but I know that it was his brother and I can describe him, but now I do not know if that is his name, if his name was Dzafo or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you agreed with Ms. Residovic that it was Dzafo, you were just kind of speculating or guessing, is that right? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for sure, and the exact name I am not sure of. Sometimes I make mistakes with my closest neighbour, but I can describe him now, how he walked and all that. That I know, because I was very close to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the question was, when you agreed with Mr.s Residovic that that was Dzafo, you were just speculating, right? You were just guessing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I do not think it has been answered, Judge, I think it has been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not certain whether it was Dzafo, whether Dzafo was his name, but I know that it was his brother, that I know for 100 per cent. I knew about Sefik very well and I could not be wrong about his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is fine. Sir, going back to the defence of Bradina. As I understand your testimony, there was no organisation -- there was not a military commander and there was not uniforms for the people defending Bradina, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any uniforms, because I think that I was -- even if anything was being done, I was not agreeing with that. I do not agree even today, so I know very little about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know, like I say, of any military organisation with a commander and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities, when I was taken prisoner, they also knew what I am saying even now, how I was, I am talking only about myself, I cannot speak of others. I think that it was very clear to them and Jasna Dzumhur even told my wife "we know that he is not guilty of anything" and they worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as I recall from your testimony with Ms. Residovic yesterday, you were one of the more prominent citizens of Bradina, or you were; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I had, I had a lot, I had a butcher's shop, a slaughterhouse, my own restaurant, my own stores. I do not know if I was the most prominent or what, but I was known as a good person and I assisted everyone, regardless of whether somebody was a Croat or Muslim or Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine and I appreciate that, sir. You had this large, for lack of a better word, investment; you had two houses in Bradina, all your businesses. You had a lot going for you in Bradina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not really a company altogether, they were separate businesses, and I had one shop in Brdjani, one cluster was the butcher's shop and the store and the restaurant. I also had an apartment in Konjic right next to the Post Office building, and then I had a different shop in Brdjani, so that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, back in April, May, maybe March, this whole area of 1992, in Bradina, you all had televisions, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was very rarely, because I did not have time, I had a lot of work. People from Repovci, Sokolovic, Sunji, from all these villages they would all come to me, up until the last day and whoever came I gave to all three people -- people of all three sides, without any distinction, depending on what religion they were of. So I was just conducting my business, Kisa came and said "you are just thinking of your business", that is all you do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had televisions and I bet you had radio and newspapers also, did you not, sir, access to those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had access to all those things, but I was not following it, because I had business and somebody had to conduct this business. You always had to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the news was full of news about fighting and your country breaking up and things like that, people arming themselves; you remember all that was in the news, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, I can tell you we did not have much of television, because you could not get the -- you could not catch the images, there were no relays, so you could not watch it, you could not get the picture very well. There was no relay that really covered that area, you could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, maybe you can help me with this, and this is what I am trying to get at; you are obviously not the first person to testify here from Bradina and I suspect you will not be the last person who is a Bradina resident, or was. Pretty much uniformly, they have told us that they really were not paying much attention to what was going on. Some people are more interested in the news and some things like that than others, but let me suggest to you, sir, that if my country were arming itself and Texas was splitting off from Oklahoma and we were about set to start a war, a war might be about to break out, I suspect that I would be pretty interested in what is going on. And you, as a person of some wealth who had a lot to lose in a war -- in fact you lost everything, did you not, in the war? You lost your two houses and your slaughterhouse and your restaurant and all of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would just -- sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The apartment, too. I lost everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, maybe you can help me with this. What is it about, not just you, but the other people in Bradina that when all these events, these cataclysmic events in your country are occurring, nobody pays any attention to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think now I am talking about myself, I cannot talk for others. I personally was fine with everyone Zukici, everywhere, and I thought I could never do to somebody with whom I sat in Repovci to his children or his wife, I never thought that something like this could happen, not even remotely, but if the situation were reversed, if I were commanding -- in a commander position like some people were, I do not think that I ever could have done things that they did, and I do not like to talk about it because when I do not think about it, I forget everything, because these are all very bad memories. I kept a restaurant, so most of these guards, Mirso and Spiljak who came to Tarcin when I was there, when I was brought to the silo, those were people who came and sat down with me 100 times, more than 100 times. If I see that he drank too much, I drive him home, I gave them money when they needed it for their wedding or when their father died. I could not understand that and I still cannot understand today that something like that could have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is you really did not pay attention to all of these events that were occurring in your country and in your area simply because you thought that nothing bad would happen; is that pretty much what you are saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I thought that this war would never take place, so I was always in my stores because I had to be there, it was a lot of work, it is not small job to have, the restaurant, the stores, the slaughterhouse. If you want to do it well, you have to be there all the time, and just to add, there was -- Vesna who was working there and she was Croatian and I made no distinction between her and my sister and she worked there for seven years. Had I treated her badly, she would not have stayed for seven years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people would come into your stores and your restaurant and you would deal with the public every day, right? You are in the retail business.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were very few people from Sarajevo who would not come down to my shop and get meat there. It always had fresh meat, it was on the main highway. I think that there were very few people from Sarajevo, from Hadzici, Tuzla, Zenica, even Belgrade, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you dealt with the public every day; that is what you do in the retail business. Did you not hear people talking about these events going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes some people would say, maybe there will be war, when it happened in Croatia, they say, "no, this will not happen here, it will pass us, because people in these parts, they would not fight each other", so people would say that something could happen, but not in this area, it will pass this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will pass the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not know if you want to, we have ten minutes, would you like to break early? I can ask some questions now if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, we can take the break at 11.30. Cross-examined by MS. McMURREY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. J.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to let you know, I am the last Defence counsel to question you, and if we have an agreement like the one with Mr. Moran, that you listen to the question and try to only answer the question I am asking, then we will both be finished here pretty quickly. Is that an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also I am sure that the Prosecutor had spoken to you earlier about only testifying about things you have personal knowledge of, so if we can have another agreement that when I ask you a question you will not answer to what you heard, but you will only answer what you personally experienced or witnessed; is that an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I forgot to introduce myself. I am Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Mr. Landzo. Just an overview here; you made what is equivalent to about four statements before testifying here today, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one would have been the one on June 9th 1992, to the Territorial Defence and MUP while you were in Celebici; that one. You acknowledge that one, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I was detained, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was June 1992. The second one was February 8th 1993, you gave a statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre to someone named Ksenija Lukic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the name was, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third one would have been on October 20th 1995 to Mr. Regis Abribat with the OTP, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. From here, you mean the investigators, is that who you are referring to? I do not know who you are referring to. What year was this? I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was October 1995 and it was the representative of the Prosecutor's office, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you signed a fourth statement on February 21st 1996 with another representative of the Prosecutor's office, where you stated that you had an opportunity to review your statement of 1995 and that everything you said in that statement from 1995 was true and correct to the best of your knowledge; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know. I do not remember that. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not remember having them come ask you to sign an affidavit and an acknowledgment, and signing one for a Mr. Ole Hortemo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is what happened. I think he did come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are looking at four different statements. I want to go to another subject; how long have you been in The Hague, Mr. J?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In The Hague, I have been here since last Saturday. I do not know what day it is today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the other witnesses that have come to testify here for the Prosecution have been accompanied by an escort from the Association of Detainees. Have you been accompanied by one of these escorts from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had no escort from the Association of Detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know who they are, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a person with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a person that travelled to The Hague with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do not mind, I do not know whether we need to go in private session or not, is that person a family member or is that an escort from wherever you come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how you think about it, a man came and then I went with him, a man came, we went, he said, "would you go to The Hague and I am going too", so we are going together. That is how we got here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think I can clear this up, Ms. McHenry. Is this person you are referring to a person from the Tribunal or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he works for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. You also, on the statement that you gave on February 21st 1993 to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre -- that centre, is it also a branch of the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was -- I never visited this Association of Detainees in Belgrade, I was never there, so I do not know. I heard from the others that it exists, that this Association of Detainees exists, but I do not know what branch of what they are, but I heard from the other detainees that there is such a thing as an Association of Detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for just one second. I have a question I need to ask, I am not quite sure whether this person is still protected or not. He was at one time and I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for this purpose? (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: After you were examined, Mr. J, you were allowed to take your X-rays and your urine reports and your blood work with you, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the doctor examined me, he sent me to another hospital to see a psychiatrist, I cannot remember exactly the name of the hospital, I know I went to see a psychiatrist who examined me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. J, the question was, when you were examined and you left the hospital, you were allowed to take a copy of your X-rays and your blood report with you, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You did not ask whether he even had X-rays. You assumed he had?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I did not. Mr. J, you did have X-rays and blood work done during your examination? And please do not mention the name of the doctor, because we are back in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you were exchanged in November, you were taken directly to Belgrade, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one took me there, I went there myself, immediately, because I did not want to stay there, to kill poor people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. J, can you tell us what the Serbian Counsel Information Centre is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what it is. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who sent you to them to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, somebody -- I went there and made a statement. Who it was -- I cannot remember who it was, this was a long time ago in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not remember how you found this place to make a statement then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there giving a statement, were there other detainees there making statements to this counsel also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other detainees there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other detainees that gave statements to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I have no idea, they probably did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the address of the Serbian Counsel Information Centre in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you the address of the flat I stayed in in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who else you have discussed your experiences at Celebici with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean, "who else".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean after you were released from Celebici, it would be natural if you and some of the other detainees got together to -- even a psychological or emotional relief, to discuss what happened and what occurred at Celebici. Were you afforded that luxury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, while I was in Belgrade, I only met with Janko. The other detainees were not there, I doubt it, maybe some of them were, but I did not meet with them to talk about it, because my sister rented a flat for me in New Belgrade. I do not recall the exact address, it was close to a marketplace, and I stayed there for a while, until -- that is how it was. I was there for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I am going to go on to a different subject now. I believe you stated in all of your statements that you lived in Bradina, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Bradina, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated yesterday in your testimony that Maca had a flat next to yours in Konjic and you told us today that you had a flat in Konjic close to the post office; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. There was one metre between our two doors. I had two houses in Bradina and an apartment in Konjic, in the centre, near the post office. I do not remember the exact address. Maca and Makaron, these two brothers, lived next door. It is the same entrance only two apartments, one next to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you lived on 15th September Street, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Konjic, your flat was on 15th September Street in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was its name, just behind the post office. Whether it is 15th September Street I do not know, I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your balcony faced the post office, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Landzo family lived on the fourth floor of the neighbouring apartment building right next to you, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that, as I was working in Bradina, my wife and children lived there for a while, and then the women and children moved to Bradina as well, so that I heard that he was working there and that his mother was there, who had lived in the -- who had worked in the municipality where my wife had also worked, but personally, I did not know him, I did not have any personal contact with him. I may have met him in the street and seen him, but when I got to the camp, (redacted) (redacetd)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. J, remember how we talked about not testifying about what you heard from somebody else about, only about what you personally know; we have, we have an agreement about that, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth about the flat in Konjic is that while you were in Celebici and before the war, your wife and your two daughters -- who, by the way, at that time were about the same age as two of my daughters -- lived at the flat in Konjic, did they not; in fact your daughter -- I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My only objection would be she has already stated that she does not want this witness to state what he heard from others, and since the question assumes that he was detained in Celebici, I will just note, in fairness to the witness, that he cannot answer this question from his own personal knowledge, so I would either object or ask Defence counsel to withdraw her request that everything he testifies to has to be something he witnessed himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I agree, and I believe this witness knows where his family was while he was detained at Celebici and I will ask him if he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. J, your family lived on 15th September Street before the war and your children attended school at the Musala school called Zvonimir Belesa-Nono at Musala, did they not, before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My children for a time before the war, long before the war, they lived in the apartment in Konjic and from somewhere, 1988 onwards, they lived in Bradina and they went to school in Bradina, because there was a school nearby, an elementary school right nearby. My older daughter went to Konjic by bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So your older daughter went to school in Konjic and while -- if you know, while you were detained in Celebici, your family stayed in the flat in Konjic, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was detained in Celebici, my family for a short period, because my family was captured in Bradina, taken to Musala, and then I remember well the name, because my wife told me, somebody called Ivica Bosnjak, who was a policeman before the war, came to take them out and took them to the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is yes, they did stay in the flat in Konjic, as far as you know, while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You not only had a butcher's shop in Bradina, you also had a butcher's shop in Konjic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have a butcher's shop in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now I am going to go to a different topic also. Before you arrived at Celebici, you were beaten, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
